author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Two deeply personal films premiered at the Cannes Film Festival, telling stories of childhood shaped by war, displacement and survival.

“Duera,” set in Kosovo during the late 1990s, follows a 13-year-old girl navigating adolescence as conflict with Serbia looms. Director Blerta Basholli says the film reflects her own experiences growing up during uncertainty and focuses on the innocence of youth rather than politics.

Another film, “Congo Boy,” tells the story of a teenage refugee from the Democratic Republic of Congo living through conflict in the Central African Republic. Based on director Nelson Makengo’s own life, the film explores survival, family responsibility and the hope young refugees carry despite war.

Both films premiered at the Cannes Film Festival as filmmakers used cinema to highlight the human cost of conflict and the fragility of childhood.
Al Jazeera's Natacha Butler reports from Cannes, France

description:
Florida has introduced a major change to its driving test system: applicants can now only take the test in English.

The move ends the use of translated exams, interpreters, and translation apps in one of the most multilingual states in the US — including Miami-Dade County, where most residents speak a language other than English at home.

Supporters say drivers must understand English road signs to improve public safety. Critics argue the policy unfairly targets immigrants and could force more unlicensed drivers onto the roads.

Driving instructors, immigrant advocates, and residents warn the new rule could make daily life harder for workers and families who rely on cars to get to work, hospitals, and schools.

The debate comes amid broader tensions over immigration policies in Florida, particularly affecting Hispanic and Haitian communities.

So is the new law about road safety — or part of a wider crackdown on immigrants?

Pakistan is facing mounting economic pressure as the war involving Iran disrupts energy exports from the Gulf.

The country depends heavily on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG) and imports around 90% of its oil and petroleum products from the region. But with supplies disrupted and prices surging, Islamabad is struggling to secure affordable energy cargoes.

The impact is already being felt across Pakistan.

But with strict IMF conditions limiting subsidies, many Pakistanis say the rising cost of living is becoming unbearable.

On the streets of Havana, opinions are sharply divided—some defending Cuba’s actions, others rejecting any prosecution of its former leadership.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Taiwan produces around 60% of the world’s semiconductors and nearly all of its most advanced chips, a dominance often described as a “silicon shield” against external threats.

But that shield is now facing pressure.

US tariff threats targeting high-tech industries, alongside concerns over Chinese attempts to acquire sensitive know-how, are raising questions about the long-term security of Taiwan’s most valuable sector.

At the same time, the island’s chip boom has deepened domestic inequality. While areas around the Hsinchu Science Park thrive, property prices have surged and wealth gaps have widened sharply, leaving many unable to keep pace with rising living costs.

As Taiwan doubles down on AI and high-performance computing, experts warn the economy is becoming even more dependent on a single industry—raising new vulnerabilities in a rapidly shifting geopolitical landscape.

So is Taiwan’s semiconductor dominance still a shield—or has it become a source of new risk?

title: Taiwan’s semiconductor “silicon shield” under pressure

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
This episode of This Is America asks what we really learn from the Pentagon’s decision to declassify decades of UFO – now UAP – files. The US Defense Department has begun uploading more than 160 files covering over 400 incidents from the 1940s to last year to a new public site, offering grainy infrared videos, ambiguous photos and eyewitness reports that have fueled generations of speculation about whether we’re alone in the universe. The documents show no evidence that the US government has encountered extraterrestrial beings or believes they have visited Earth, yet the release is being hailed as a landmark shift toward open-source analysis and data-driven transparency, with NASA pledging to “follow the data and share what we learn.” From Washington, Al Jazeera’s Richard Gaisford examines whether this transparency push actually brings us closer to the truth or just deepens the mystery.
